chunks: "The receiver wants P and N to be exact mirror images at the same instant.
If one line arrives late, then for a short time both lines are moving in the same direction, or one is moving and the other isn't, and that interval looks like common-mode instead of differential.
So skew does three bad things.
First, it converts some of your signal into common-mode, which is a voltage the receiver is designed to ignore, so you lose a bit of signal, though the loss is small.
Second, that common-mode is real current on the traces and the cable, and common-mode current radiates far better than differential current, so skew shows up as an EMI problem.
Third, it eats timing margin: the differential edge gets slower and the eye gets narrower, which means jitter at the receiver.
The quantity that matters is the ratio of skew to rise time and bit time.

At 5 gigahertz, 20 picoseconds of skew is about 3 millimetres of mismatch and gives a mode-conversion ratio of roughly minus 10 decibels in S-parameter terms, which is a common-mode voltage about a sixth of the differential amplitude.
5 picoseconds drops that to about minus 22 decibels.
To ensure they arrive together I length-match inside the pair, in time rather than millimetres, and I do it locally where the asymmetry appears: after each bend, at the breakout, around vias.
I use identical vias, symmetric AC-coupling caps and connectors, and for the fastest links I think about glass-weave skew.
Then I verify with a TDR or a differential-to-common-mode S-parameter."
